# Project documentation

Consolidated on 2026-10-24. The current research guide appears first. The source sections preserve the historical contents of the former Markdown files (with current repository, folder, and import references), including historical notes, publication drafts, license terms, and the saved session transcript. Historical claims and instructions describe their original context; use the current research guide for the active protocol and status.

README and agent guidance files remain in their original locations. Local environments, dependency files, and repository metadata are outside this documentation consolidation.

## Current research guide

# seqcredit project

This is the single documentation source for the retained synthetic credit-risk
research workflow. Use [`README.md`](../README.md) for installation; use the
code and machine-readable configuration below as the implementation authority.

## Workspace

`seqcredit` on branch `main` is the sole active research workspace. Repository and distribution: `seqcredit`; Python import: `seqcredit`. Historical source excerpts and frozen v2 contract identifiers retain their original names.
The compared legacy source is retained for reference at
`../archive/code/legacy-model/`. Dashboard, Spark,
publication, historical-data, and real-data components remain outside the
active v2 path.

## Code map

| Purpose | Source |
|---|---|
| Frozen design | [`src/configs/experiment_design.json`](../src/configs/experiment_design.json) |
| Generator, features, partitions | [`src/scripts/experiment_v2.py`](../src/scripts/experiment_v2.py) |
| Runner and models | [`src/scripts/run_smoke.py`](../src/scripts/run_smoke.py) |
| Run validator | [`src/scripts/validate_pilots.py`](../src/scripts/validate_pilots.py) |
| Matrix planner/executor | [`src/scripts/run_matrix.py`](../src/scripts/run_matrix.py) |
| Matrix validator | [`src/scripts/validate_matrix.py`](../src/scripts/validate_matrix.py) |
| Bootstrap uncertainty | [`src/scripts/bootstrap_predictions.py`](../src/scripts/bootstrap_predictions.py) |
| Contract checks | [`src/scripts/contract_checks.py`](../src/scripts/contract_checks.py) |
| Regression tests | [`src/scripts/`](../src/scripts/) and [`src/tests/`](../src/tests/) |
| Calibration evidence | [`docs/calibration/`](calibration/) |

## Reproduce

```powershell
uv sync --group dev
uv run python -m pytest
.\src\scripts\test-smoke.ps1
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe src\scripts\run_matrix.py
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe src\scripts\run_matrix.py --execute
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe src\scripts\validate_matrix.py `
  --execution data\matrix_execution.json
```

## Research question and evidence boundary

Compare static borrower aggregates with transaction sequences under
`no_signal`, `aggregate_signal`, and `order_signal` interventions. Transactions
are synthetic and informed by aggregate telco evidence; they are not
anonymized customer records and do not establish telco deployment performance.
Population distributions, transaction mechanics, timing, amounts, and loan
outcomes are explicit simulation assumptions.

The calibration ledger contains source-linked aggregate records and a
243-category mapping. Historical weights are scenario references, not
borrower-level probabilities. Do not use archived real-data rankings as
generator acceptance targets.

## Frozen v2 protocol

- Profiles: smoke 1,000 borrowers; pilot 5,000; main 25,625.
- Main split: borrower-level 60/20/20 (15,375/5,125/5,125).
- Histories: latest 32 events for smoke, 64 for pilot/main, all before day 0.
- Labels: derived from realized future events through day 60.
- Targets: primary `label == 2`; secondary `label in {1, 2}`.
- Models: logistic regression, LightGBM, and compact GRU.
- Preprocessing: fit only on inner-fit borrowers; validation/test are excluded
  from fitting and early stopping.
- Controls: retrained label permutation and retrained sequence-order shuffle.
- Artifacts: immutable run directories containing configuration, hashes, split
  IDs, inputs, models, predictions, metrics, audit checks, and manifests.

## Verified status

The complete active suite passes: **217 tests**. The preregistered matrix
contains 30 runs: 18 headline configurations and 12 retrained controls.
`data/matrix_execution.json` reports **30/30 passed**.
`matrix_validation.json`, produced by
[`src/scripts/validate_matrix.py`](../src/scripts/validate_matrix.py), reports
**30/30 independent validations passed**.

Do not choose seeds, settings, thresholds, or claims from sealed test scores.
Pilot and test metrics are recorded evidence, not tuning inputs.

## Archive decision

The newer v2 workspace was retained for explicit data boundaries, fit-only
preprocessing, borrower-level splits, immutable artifacts, controls, and
independent validation. The legacy clone is simpler but incompatible with the
v2 history, label, feature, split, and cache contract. Keep it read-only and
out of the Python module path.


Commands in the research guide run from `seqcredit/`. The source sections below retain historical context; repository, folder, and import references use the current names.

## Reference archive layout

The gitignored `archive/` is a private reference collection. It contains no
nested Git checkout, virtual environment, package installation metadata, or
agent instruction files. Archived setup instructions and dependency declarations
are captured as text in `archive/provenance/original-project-context.json`.

- `archive/code/legacy-model/`: compared legacy model source and license.
- `archive/code/legacy-configuration/`: legacy generator parameters.
- `archive/code/dashboard/` and `dashboard-tests/`: retired dashboard source and tests.
- `archive/code/dashboard-entrypoints/`: historical launchers retained as source references.
- `archive/code/retired-modules/` and `retired-tests/`: retired Spark and poster code and tests.
- `archive/code/publication-tools/`: figure generation and publication utilities.
- `archive/notebooks/`: historical notebooks and exports; calibration notebook paths and hashes remain unchanged.
- `archive/evidence/`: historical datasets, models, result tables, publications, and draft snapshots.
- `archive/provenance/`: original context, prior manifests, and the verified cleanup file map.

The archived code is for reading and comparison. Its original relative imports,
launchers, and data paths describe the historical layout. Keep it outside the
active module path. Temporary renders, LaTeX build logs, and checkout scaffolding
were removed; retained files were verified by SHA-256 during the cleanup.

## Root analysis notebooks

- [`analyze_data.ipynb`](../analyze_data.ipynb): descriptive statistics and generator-target comparisons over existing synthetic data.
- [`train_model.ipynb`](../train_model.ipynb): training and evaluation of static, LSTM, and hybrid models; saves models and arrays.
- [`analyze_result.ipy`](../analyze_result.ipy): loads saved models for explanations, secondary-target analysis, and probability calibration.

These are the older shared-data notebooks, separate from the frozen v2 runners.
Run training before result analysis. `analyze_result.ipy` retains notebook JSON
under the explicitly requested filename. Their setup locates the project from
the research root, its parent workspace, or the former notebook directory.

# Synthetic research codebase comparison

Reviewed 2026-10-24: `seqcredit` at `6322bf1` (`main`) and `seqcredit-model-real` at `2465286` (`real-data`). This is a source comparison, not a completed leakage audit or runtime validation. Neither clone was modified or merged. No datasets or saved results were regenerated.

## Recommendation

Use `seqcredit-model-real` as the consolidation base, retaining the original clone until consolidation is verified. Its name reflects its history, not a requirement to use Databricks: it already contains the same synthetic generator and the local feature pipeline. Retain its useful tests and model fixes; simplify its mixed research, Spark, publication, and presentation responsibilities. Bring across selected original improvements rather than merging branches wholesale.

Neither clone should yet be treated as an approved experimental baseline. Their shared synthetic design and evaluation boundaries still need the next audit.

## Component decisions

| Component | Observed difference | Proposed disposition |
|---|---|---|
| `synthesize.py` | Identical after normalizing CRLF/LF line endings | Retain one copy; no generator migration needed |
| `src/synthetic_params.json` | No Git content difference | Retain with provenance; generator documentation calls these real-data calibration parameters, so synthetic transactions are not automatically evidence of an independently designed simulation |
| `pipeline.py` | Same broad feature design; original collects new columns and concatenates once, newer repeatedly inserts them | Carry the original batching improvement into the retained pipeline, after checking feature equivalence |
| `config.py` | Newer supports environment overrides and DBFS-style paths | Retain configurable local paths; separate cloud-specific behavior from the default local workflow |
| `credit_model.py` | Four static models remain; newer adds GRU, Hybrid GRU, Transformer, Hybrid Transformer, raw sequence input, and additional cache logic | Retain useful fixes and model implementations; keep initial experiment scope small rather than activating every architecture |
| `run_cv_benchmark.py` | Original benchmarks LSTM and Hybrid LSTM; newer benchmarks LSTM and GRU, saves OOF predictions, supports static-only runs and runtime paths | Prefer newer output preservation and orchestration; make model selection explicit; preserve original hybrid CV routine as a reference if hybrids are later needed |
| `run_ablation_study.py`, `run_hyperparameter_tuning.py`, `compute_bootstrap_ci.py` | Identical after line-ending normalization | Keep one copy, audit their assumptions before using them |
| `reset.py`, `run_full_benchmark.py` | Identical after line-ending normalization | Keep one copy for review; do not assume identical means correct |
| Tests | Original has one source-local end-to-end smoke script; newer has a dedicated suite across generation, features, loading, models, evaluation, CLI, reset, config, exports, and Spark | Retain newer suite; separate Spark tests and strengthen scientific invariants during the audit |
| `real_data_pipeline.py`, `build_poster.py`, `app/` | Additional Spark, publication, and presentation responsibilities in newer clone | Preserve separately by purpose; exclude them from the minimal synthetic research path |

## Concrete improvements in the newer clone

- `credit_model.py:1396` fixes the original LSTM lazy-build variable typo (`input_shapes` assigned, `input_shape` used at original line 1175). This matters when calling `fit()` without explicitly building first.
- The raw-NPZ loader adds normalization fitted on non-padded training timesteps (`credit_model.py:148`) and ordered borrower alignment.
- Derived raw-sequence caches have metadata for train/test IDs, sequence length, feature names, and raw source path. This is a useful direction, though validation is incomplete.
- `run_cv_benchmark.py:564` saves OOF predictions rather than retaining them only in memory. This supports subsequent independent evaluation.
- The benchmark accepts GRU through its recurrent CV function, can run static models when sequence inputs are unavailable, and recomputes XGBoost's class ratio for each target. That ratio is still computed outside individual folds.
- Dedicated tests exercise generator reproducibility, split disjointness, loader validation, feature extraction, model fit/predict/persistence, and CLI behavior.

## Important limitations carried forward

### Cache handling is unfinished

The newer loader first validates metadata, but retains an older unconditional cache-read branch at `credit_model.py:640`. A rejected cache can therefore be loaded by the fallback when no raw NPZ takes the earlier path. The per-user CSV path also writes the older cache format at line 823. The new metadata comparison does not validate source content hashes or all stored metadata fields.

The existing loader tests explicitly document this fallback issue and work around it with explicit temporary paths (`tests/test_credit_model_data_loader.py:177`). Preserve the tests, but do not mistake that workaround for a production fix.

### A larger test suite is useful, but not scientific validation

For example, `test_scaler_fit_on_train_only` checks that transformed training features have approximately zero mean. This is a useful numerical check, but a stronger leakage test must also establish that changing held-out data cannot affect fitted preprocessing. Sequence tests include real one-epoch fit/predict/save/load checks, but explicitly build the models first, so they do not exercise every entry path.

The original end-to-end script is also limited: it builds a hybrid model and makes an untrained prediction rather than validating trained predictive behavior. It uses a fixed `test_sandbox` location and deletes that directory on entry. It should not be transplanted unchanged.

### Both share unresolved experiment-design assumptions

The generator's final user label is the maximum loan-risk label encountered during generation (`synthesize.py:623`), while the feature-building entry point reads each user's transaction file without an explicit prediction cutoff. The next audit must define the prediction moment and distinguish observed history from future outcomes.

Both CSV-based sequence loaders fit scaling on the outer training users before the benchmark subdivides those users into CV folds. Both recurrent CV routines use the scoring fold as explicit validation data for early stopping. These observations are audit leads, not a complete account of all leakage routes.

The shared full-benchmark wrapper deletes existing result/cache files before running and refers to `cv_results_bad.csv`, whereas the main benchmark writes `cv_results_y_bad.csv`. It should be replaced or repaired as part of establishing a reliable run command, not used blindly.

### Dependencies and imports need separation

Both projects require Python `>=3.13,<3.14`, use the same package name/version, and eagerly import model code from `__init__.py`. Both model modules import TensorFlow and multiple model dependencies at module import time, so even lightweight use is coupled to the heavy stack.

The newer `pyproject.toml` additionally bundles Spark, PowerPoint/PDF generation, and Streamlit/chart dependencies with research dependencies. It pins scikit-learn to 1.8.0 while its `requirements.txt` leaves that package unpinned; `python-pptx` is declared in pyproject but absent from requirements. Keep a single authoritative environment definition, with optional groups for cloud, app, and publication work. This comparison did not check package compatibility or current upstream releases.

## Proposed retained foundation

1. Shared synthetic generator and parameters, with a documented simulation contract.
2. One local feature pipeline, carrying over the original batching improvement.
3. The newer loader/configuration as a starting point, with one cache path and explicit dataset provenance after audit.
4. The four existing static model implementations and recurrent implementations preserved, but an initial runnable experiment limited to a static baseline and one recurrent model.
5. Newer test infrastructure, split into local research and optional integration tests.
6. Benchmark output preservation from the newer runner, extended later with borrower IDs, split membership, fitted preprocessing, source/config hashes, and separate run directories.

Keep the presentation app and historical real-data materials as separate concerns. The demo's metric-calibrated surrogate is not the synthetic research foundation.

## Next step

Audit the retained synthetic path in execution order: generator and label semantics → observation cutoff → borrower alignment and splitting → preprocessing and caches → CV and early stopping → result export. Resolve the prediction task before running a new headline benchmark. Only then consolidate source and retire the older checkout/environment.

## Verification performed

Compared source inventories, normalized file contents, targeted diffs, dependency declarations, package exports, test fixtures and test bodies. Git content comparison found no generator-parameter difference. Working trees were clean at the start of this comparison. No training, package installation, or test execution was performed; runtime compatibility and test pass status remain unverified.

# Codex conversation

## User

never has a project like this stretched me and helped me grow. but in the process, it has also costed me a lot of headache. initially we struggle to get data for 6 months. then we had access but only through databricks. so every run we had to commit code, pull it in and run the code. now there are data leakage problems because we normalized before splitting and we didn't see it till we lost access to the data permanently. I want us to go back to synthetic data. but this time I want us to clean up and a lot of the mess and this directory and maintain lean development. first things first inspect the folders. some of them our branches and some are also just cosmetic, others are for reference but let's go throughly and let's work our way up to getting the tidying up done

## Assistant

I’ll inspect the folder structure, Git branches and worktrees, and project guidance first. Then I’ll map what appears active, reference-only, generated, or redundant so we can tidy it in stages. I won’t move or delete anything during this inspection.

    # Sequential Credit Risk Modeling - Consolidated Project Reference
    
    **Author:** Benjamin Ekow Attabra
    **Last updated:** 2026-09-02
    
    This file is the authoritative overview for status, research direction,
    evidence boundaries, workspace selection, publication handoff, and the planned
    presentation MVP across the local projects in this `yara/` folder. Repo-local
    documentation remains the source for setup and implementation details.
    
    ---
    
    ## TL;DR
    
    - **Primary research focus:** credit-risk modeling, not general user-behavior
      interpretation.
    - **Central question:** can transaction-level sequential models predict credit
      default more accurately, reliably, and usefully than models built from
      aggregate Mobile Financial Services (MFS) features?
    - **Active workspace:** `seqcredit-model-real/` on the `real-data` branch.
      The older `seqcredit/` checkout is the synthetic proof-of-concept and
      should not be used for current real-data claims.
    - **Target venue:** [Africa in AI 2026](https://africainai.mailab.io/), a
      NeurIPS 2026 affinity workshop. The full-paper deadline is **September 10,
      2026 at 11:59 PM Anywhere on Earth**.
    - **Current evidence:** preserved executed Databricks notebooks consistently
      show GRU/LSTM outperforming static models on default discrimination, while
      static tree models are better calibrated for strict default.
    - **Supervisor status:** permission to proceed with the submission has been
      confirmed. Exact method facts must now be recovered from the surviving
      archive rather than requested from the supervisor.
    - **Critical constraint:** the raw and derived real-data assets are no longer
      accessible in Databricks or locally. The project can support an archival
      empirical paper only where the notebooks and code preserve sufficient
      provenance; it cannot currently support new real-data experiments or full
      reproduction from source.
    - **Paper boundary:** observed transaction behavior is model input and an
      interpretability aid. The paper does not claim to explain users, infer
      psychological traits, or establish causal behavioral mechanisms.
    - **Research closeout:** the evidence freeze, anonymous manuscript rebuild, and
      PDF verification are complete within the surviving archive's limitations.
      OpenReview submission is the only remaining publication action.
    - **Presentation MVP:** an isolated `seqcredit-model-real/app/` prototype now demonstrates
      batch credit-risk scoring on fabricated records. It is not a production
      lending system and does not present demo scores as real Telecel predictions.
    
    ## Status update - September 2, 2026
    
    - **Publication package:** complete and frozen. The anonymous nine-page PDF,
      manuscript source, evidence ledger, and private backup remain in place; no new
      research or manuscript changes have been made since the August 27 closeout.
    - **Repository state:** `seqcredit-model-real/` is clean on `real-data` at
      commit `722629a`; the superseded synthetic checkout is clean on `main` at
      commit `6322bf1`. The root `yara/` workspace is not itself a Git repository.
    - **Submission:** pending. The official schedule still lists the full-paper
      deadline as **September 10, 2026 at 11:59 PM AoE**, eight calendar days after
      this status date. Uploading the anonymous PDF through OpenReview is the only
      remaining action required for the research submission.
    - **Data recovery:** unchanged and deferred. The missing real-data tables and
      fitted artifacts have not been restored, and the frozen claim boundary still
      applies.
    - **Presentation MVP:** first end-to-end prototype complete in
      `seqcredit-model-real/app/`. The calibrated synthetic benchmark reproduces the
      broad archived ranking (static AUC 0.729; order-aware AUC 0.755), and the
      offline dashboard supports sample loading, CSV validation/scoring, portfolio
      and borrower views, benchmark comparison, and CSV export. Its sequence model
      is an explicitly labeled order-aware surrogate, not a GRU or LSTM.
    
    ---
    
    ## Research direction
    
    ### Primary research question
    
    > Do transaction-level sequential models improve credit-risk prediction over
    > aggregate behavioral features in a large, data-constrained Ghanaian MFS
    > setting, and what discrimination-calibration trade-off results?
    
    The project should answer a credit-risk modeling question. User behavior is
    relevant only insofar as transaction records contain predictive signal for a
    defined credit outcome.
    
    ### Supporting questions
    
    1. Do GRU and LSTM models outperform logistic regression and tree-based static
       baselines under the same leakage-aware cohort design?
    2. Is the observed sequential-model advantage stable across preserved reruns?
    3. How does stronger default discrimination trade off against probability
       calibration?
    4. Which aggregate feature groups contribute signal to the strongest static
       baseline?
    5. What can and cannot be concluded in the absence of temporal, calibration,
       subgroup, and decision-utility extensions?
    
    ### Scope boundaries
    
    The paper may report that a feature or sequence contains predictive signal. It
    must not present model importance as proof of why people behave as they do.
    
    Use cautious language such as:
    
    - "transaction-type composition contains predictive signal"
    - "recipient diversity may proxy network breadth"
    - "sequential models capture information discarded by aggregation"
    
    Avoid unsupported claims such as:
    
    - "recipient diversity measures social capital"
    - "airtime purchasing proves liquidity stress"
    - "the model explains borrower behavior"
    - causal, psychological, demographic, or anthropological conclusions derived
      only from feature importance or SHAP values
    
    The phrase "financial anthropology" should not be a central contribution.

    ## Publication target: Africa in AI 2026
    
    ### Venue fit
    
    Africa in AI 2026 emphasizes locally grounded African AI, low-resource and
    high-impact work, data sovereignty, responsible AI, practical infrastructure,
    and routes from research to fintech deployment. This makes it a stronger fit
    than the previously considered IAAI framing for an empirical Ghanaian MFS
    credit-risk study.
    
    Official links:
    
    - Workshop: <https://africainai.mailab.io/>
    - Submission instructions: <https://africainai.mailab.io/how-to-submit>
    - OpenReview: <https://openreview.net/group?id=NeurIPS.cc/2026/Workshop/Africa_in_AI>
    
    ### Submission requirements
    
    - Full paper: 8 pages of content plus up to 2 pages of references
    - Format: official Springer LNCS template, submitted as PDF
    - Review: double-blind
    - Originality: not previously published in another venue, proceeding, or
      journal
    - Eligibility: at least one researcher working or studying in Africa
    - Supplementary material: permitted where it clarifies methodology
    - Recommended content: compute resources, data splits, inference time, and
      impact in African contexts
    - Full-paper deadline: **September 10, 2026, 11:59 PM AoE**
    - Acceptance notification: September 20, 2026
    - Camera-ready deadline: November 6, 2026
    - Event: December 6-12, 2026, Sydney and online
    
    The organizers state that they are coordinating with Springer toward an LNCS
    conference volume. Do not describe LNCS publication as guaranteed until the
    organizers confirm it.
    
    ### Working title
    
    > **Static Aggregates or Transaction Sequences? Credit Risk Modeling on
    > Ghanaian Mobile Financial Services Data**
    
    ### Planned contribution statement
    
    1. A leakage-aware protocol for credit-risk modeling from Ghanaian MFS
       transactions.
    2. A real-data comparison of aggregate and transaction-sequence models on a
       large borrower cohort.
    3. Preserved multi-run evidence that GRU models improve default discrimination
       over static baselines.
    4. An explicit discrimination-calibration analysis relevant to responsible
       lending.
    5. A reproducible synthetic companion and a transparent account of the
       infrastructure and data-governance limits surrounding proprietary African
       financial data.
    
    The paper should not claim a novel neural architecture, a general performance
    ceiling, temporal generalization, causal behavioral insight, or deployment
    readiness.

    ## Real-data study and preserved findings
    
    ### Cohort recorded by the executed notebooks
    
    - Raw Databricks table: 374,295,424 rows x 12 columns
    - Borrowers with at least one loan and at least 60 days of follow-up: 149,667
    - Labels: 51,105 good / 92,392 risky-late / 6,170 default
    - Matched feature and label users used for modeling: 149,204
    - Sequence tensor before the train/test split: 149,667 x 100 x 19
    - Leakage control: features strictly precede the index loan; labels follow the
      index loan
    
    The reported benchmark is five-fold cross-validation on the 119,363-user
    development portion created by an initial 80/20 split of the 149,204 matched
    users. The reserved 29,841-user test portion was not used. Static scaling was
    fitted within each fold, but sequence normalization preceded the folds and
    XGBoost's class ratio used the complete development target. Each recurrent
    fold also used its evaluation fold for early stopping before scoring that same
    fold. The recurrent results are therefore descriptive and potentially
    optimistic, not unbiased prospective estimates.
    
    The old manuscript's approximately 90-day, September-November description is
    contradicted by the preserved 8,466-row raw-table export, which contains records
    from September 1, 2025 through February 28, 2026. The old notebook EDA also
    computed `min` and `max` on the unparsed `DD-MON-YY` timestamp string, so its
    displayed bounds are lexicographic and invalid. The exact full-table endpoints
    remain unrecovered; see `seqcredit-model-real/docs/evidence-ledger.md`. Do not
    publish an exact duration until a parsed full-table boundary is recovered.
    
    The real-data outcome definitions are recoverable from the stable pipeline:
    
    - the index loan is each borrower's most recent qualifying disbursement
    - 60 days is a minimum eligibility follow-up, not a fixed outcome horizon
    - `good` means post-index repayment with no post-index penalty
    - `risky / late` means post-index repayment plus a post-index penalty
    - `default` means no observed post-index principal or interest repayment
    
    The last category is an operational no-repayment proxy, not a provider-verified
    contractual default or days-past-due definition.
    
    ### Canonical benchmark evidence
    
    Use **Analysis Notebook B** as the canonical real-data benchmark. Its completed
    execution is the source for the headline result:
    
    - `y_default`: GRU 0.7517 AUC-ROC; LSTM 0.7418; XGBoost 0.7211;
      RandomForest 0.7207; LightGBM 0.7193; LogisticRegression 0.7058
    - GRU and LSTM provide stronger default discrimination than the static
      baselines.
    - RandomForest and the boosting models have better Brier and ECE values than
      GRU/LSTM for strict default.
    - For `y_bad`, the calibration ordering differs; do not generalize the strict
      default calibration claim to both targets.
    
    Use **Analysis Notebook C** only as supporting rerun evidence. Its benchmark
    reports GRU 0.7530 and LSTM 0.7422 on `y_default`, preserving the same ranking.
    Do not use Notebook C's ablation results.
    
    Use **Analysis Notebook A** for the static feature-group ablation. Its coherent
    RandomForest analysis indicates that transaction-type mix and amount
    statistics produce the largest drop-one-group signal. Temporal-pattern and
    loan-history groups add little incremental static signal in that run.
    
    ### Evidence-quality rules
    
    1. Treat Notebook B as the primary run and Notebook C as a robustness rerun.
    2. Do not merge metrics from different runs into a single table.
    3. Do not use Notebook C's ablation: its ablation baseline is inconsistent
       with its own main benchmark.
    4. Do not treat the tracked `data/cv_results_*.csv` files as trustworthy
       fold-level evidence. AUC-ROC, AUC-PR, and F1 are repeated identically across
       folds and the headline values differ from Notebook B.
    5. The saved significance table contains duplicated comparisons and its
       underlying out-of-fold predictions are missing. Significance findings may
       be described as archived output, but they should not be the paper's central
       support and must not be presented as independently reverified.
    6. Do not report confidence intervals or fold-level variation that cannot be
       reconstructed from preserved evidence.
    7. Keep every paper number linked to its notebook, cell/output, and Git commit
       in an evidence ledger.

    ## Synthetic benchmark's role
    
    The synthetic stage is a reproducible companion, not a substitute for the lost
    real data.
    
    Its role in the paper is to show that:
    
    - the data-generation, feature-engineering, and evaluation code can be audited
      locally;
    - static features dominated in the calibrated simulation;
    - the real-data result reverses that ordering, demonstrating that synthetic
      structure can misrepresent the value of transaction order.
    
    Present synthetic and real results sequentially and in separate tables. Never
    imply that rerunning the synthetic benchmark reproduces the Telecel findings.

    ## Defensible claim boundary
    
    ### The paper may claim
    
    - A leakage-aware real-data experiment was completed on the recorded Telecel
      cohort.
    - Across preserved complete executions, GRU consistently ranked first on
      `y_default` AUC-ROC at approximately 0.752-0.753 in the canonical and rerun
      notebooks.
    - Sequential models improved default discrimination over aggregate baselines
      by approximately 0.03 AUC-ROC in the canonical run.
    - Static models were better calibrated for the rare strict-default target.
    - Synthetic and real data produced different static-versus-sequential model
      rankings.
    - The real-data result is limited to one provider and the preserved evaluation
      design.
    
    ### The paper must not claim
    
    - full real-data reproducibility from the released repository
    - temporal or cross-provider generalization
    - deployment readiness or improved lending profitability
    - validated fairness across demographic groups
    - causal explanations of borrower behavior
    - a new neural architecture or general performance ceiling
    - confidence intervals, fold statistics, or recalibrated probabilities that
      are not preserved

    ## Presentation MVP - implemented prototype
    
    ### Objective
    
    Build a small, offline-friendly dashboard that demonstrates the end-to-end
    credit-risk scoring flow for a presentation: upload transactions, validate the
    input, construct model inputs, score borrowers, inspect results, and export a
    scored file.
    
    The implementation is isolated in `seqcredit-model-real/app/`, alongside the
    active research checkout but separate from its core package.
    
    ### Current implementation status
    
    - A deterministic generator creates 4,500 fabricated borrowers with 162,000
      transactions and a 4.13% strict-default prevalence.
    - Five-fold out-of-fold evaluation reports 0.729 AUC-ROC for the aggregate
      RandomForest and 0.755 for an order-aware sequence surrogate, a 0.027 gain.
      These values reproduce the broad demonstration target, not the real dataset.
    - Versioned static and sequence artifacts, their hashes, feature contracts,
      acceptance bands, and demo risk-band thresholds are frozen in
      `seqcredit-model-real/app/artifacts/manifest.json`.
    - The supplied 60-borrower CSV runs through the scoring contract and local
      dashboard. Invalid schemas return concise validation errors.
    - The dashboard provides portfolio summary, score distribution, demo risk-band
      mix, borrower indicators and recent timeline, archived-real-versus-synthetic
      comparison, batch results, and CSV export.
    - The September 2 dashboard revision uses a simple white-and-violet,
      upload-first workspace for recording a demo video. It analyzes one fabricated
      borrower through visible validation/scoring stages and four tabs: overview,
      loan scenario, transactions, and model comparison. The requested-loan curve
      is explicitly labeled as a synthetic what-if index because loan amount is not
      an input to the frozen model.
    - A restrained UI refinement keeps that workflow intact while adding warmer
      neutral surfaces, quieter violet accents, plain-language copy, accessible
      focus states, clearer upload affordances, and borrower/date context without
      decorative animation or marketing-style presentation elements.
    - Six automated tests pass. The local server, health endpoint, complete demo
      payload, and invalid-upload path were exercised successfully.
    - The current interface restores batch score context and CSV export, adds a
      careful plain-language interpretation layer, and presents synthetic model
      output as a 0-100 pattern index rather than an individual default probability.
    - A browser screenshot inspection could not be performed because no browser
      control surface was available in the verification session; manual visual
      rehearsal remains before the live presentation.
    
    ### Hard boundary
    
    The surviving real-data evidence cannot supply a deployable model: the fitted
    real models, preprocessing objects, raw data, and derived real-data matrices are
    missing. The MVP must therefore use synthetic or explicitly fabricated records
    and display a persistent **prototype / not for lending decisions** notice.
    
    It must not:
    
    - describe synthetic scores as Telecel or real-borrower predictions;
    - issue approve/decline decisions;
    - claim calibrated real-world probabilities, fairness, profitability, or
      deployment readiness;
    - expose direct or hashed financial identifiers in presentation material.
    
    ### Minimum scope
    
    1. Accept one documented borrower-transaction CSV format.
    2. Validate required columns, types, timestamps, missing values, and transaction
       ordering before scoring.
    3. Reuse the existing aggregate feature concepts and extract a compact set of
       order-aware trend features behind a stable scoring interface.
    4. Load versioned synthetic preprocessing and model artifacts rather than train
       during a presentation.
    5. Return a score, a clearly labeled demo risk band, model version, and scoring
       timestamp for each borrower.
    6. Provide three compact dashboard views:
       - portfolio summary with counts, risk-band distribution, and score histogram;
       - borrower detail with score, aggregate indicators, and recent transaction
         timeline;
       - static-versus-sequential comparison when both artifacts are available.
    7. Export the scored batch as CSV.
    8. Ship with a small fabricated sample file and a single local startup command.
    
    ### Minimal architecture
    
    ```text
    CSV upload
        -> schema validation
        -> aggregate features / order-aware trend features
        -> versioned static model / sequence surrogate
        -> demo scores and risk bands
        -> dashboard and CSV export
    ```
    
    ### Build order
    
    1. Scaffold `seqcredit-model-real/app/` independently of the research package.
       **Complete.**
    2. Freeze the input schema and create a fabricated presentation dataset.
       **Complete.**
    3. Extract only the required feature and sequence code behind a stable scoring
       interface. **Complete for the order-aware v1 surrogate.**
    4. Train synthetic demo artifacts once and save the scaler, feature order,
       thresholds, model file, and manifest together. **Complete for v1.**
    5. Build batch scoring and validation tests before the interface. **Complete.**
    6. Add the dashboard views and export path. **Complete.**
    7. Package the app for offline execution and rehearse the full upload-to-export
       presentation flow. **Implementation complete; manual visual rehearsal pending.**
    
    ### MVP completion criteria
    
    - A clean environment can start the dashboard with one documented command.
    - The supplied sample scores successfully without network access.
    - Invalid schemas fail with clear, nontechnical messages.
    - Every displayed score identifies the model version and synthetic-demo status.
    - The portfolio, borrower, comparison, and export flows work end to end.
    - No real financial identifiers or restricted data are included.
    
    ### Requirements for a genuine production pilot
    
    The dashboard becomes a production candidate only after governed real data and
    model artifacts are restored or recreated, followed by fold-safe retraining,
    untouched test evaluation, calibration and threshold selection, temporal and
    fairness testing, decision-utility analysis, security controls, audit logging,
    monitoring, human-review rules, and provider/regulatory approval.

    # AGENTS.md
    
    Guidance for agentic coding agents working in this repository.
    
    ## Setup
    
    ```bash
    # Create and activate virtual environment
    python -m venv .venv
    .venv\Scripts\activate        # Windows
    # source .venv/bin/activate   # macOS/Linux
    
    # Install dependencies
    pip install -r requirements.txt
    pip install -e .              # editable install — required for python -m and notebook imports
    ```
    
    ## Running Code
    
    **Main notebook (entry point):**
    ```bash
    jupyter notebook notebooks/model.ipynb
    ```
    
    **Full pipeline (generates transactions, labels, and features):**
    ```bash
    # Step 1: Generate synthetic transaction data + labels
    python -m seqcredit.synthesize
    
    # Step 2: Build user-level features from transactions
    python -m seqcredit.pipeline
    
    # Step 3: Run the modeling notebook
    jupyter notebook notebooks/model.ipynb
    ```
    
    **Incremental updates:**
    - Rebuild only features: `python -m seqcredit.pipeline`
    - Rebuild only transactions (regenerates both transactions and labels): `python -m seqcredit.synthesize`
    
    ## Lint & Typecheck
    
    ```bash
    # Linting and formatting
    ruff check src/
    ruff format src/
    
    # Type checking
    mypy src/ --ignore-missing-imports
    ```
    
    ## Tests
    
    No test suite exists.
    
    ## Code Style
    
    ### Imports
    
    Organize imports: stdlib → third-party → local. Use try/except for local imports:
    
    ```python
    from pathlib import Path
    from typing import Tuple, Dict, List, Optional
    
    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd
    
    try:
        from seqcredit.config import USER_FEATURES_FILE
    except ModuleNotFoundError:
        from config import USER_FEATURES_FILE
    ```
    
    ### Type Hints
    
    Required for public functions. Use standard library types and numpy/pandas:
    
    ```python
    def load_static_data(self) -> Tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.Series]:
        ...
    
    def predict_proba(self, X) -> np.ndarray:
        ...
    
    def _compute_class_weights(y: np.ndarray) -> Dict[int, float]:
        ...
    ```
    
    ### Docstrings
    
    Use triple-quoted Google-style docstrings:
    
    ```python
    def extract_all_features(self, df, windows=[3, 7, 14, 30]):
        """
        Extract complete feature set from transaction sequence.
    
        Args:
            df: DataFrame with columns [TRANSACTION DATE, AMOUNT, TRANS. TYPE,
                BAL BEFORE, BAL AFTER, etc.]
            windows: List of rolling window sizes (in days)
    
        Returns:
            DataFrame with engineered features
        """
        ...
    ```
    
    ### Naming Conventions
    
    - **Functions/variables**: `snake_case` (e.g., `load_static_data`, `train_indices`)
    - **Classes**: `PascalCase` (e.g., `CreditRiskDataLoader`, `LSTMModel`)
    - **Constants**: `UPPER_CASE` (e.g., `RANDOM_SEED`, `LSTM_FEATURE_COLUMNS`)
    - **Private methods**: Prefix with underscore (e.g., `_engineer_loan_features`)
    
    ### Module Structure
    
    Define constants at top, then classes, then standalone functions:
    
    ```python
    RANDOM_SEED = 42
    LSTM_FEATURE_COLUMNS = [...]
    
    class MyClass:
        ...
    
    def standalone_function():
        ...
    
    if __name__ == "__main__":
        main()
    ```
    
    ### Error Handling
    
    Use try/except with specific exceptions. Print warnings for recoverable errors:
    
    ```python
    try:
        df_user = pd.read_csv(filepath)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  [SKIP] {user_id}: could not read file ({e})")
        continue
    ```
    
    ### Logging
    
    Currently uses `print()` for output. Continue that pattern for progress messages:
    
    ```python
    print(f"Processed {i+1}/{total} users...")
    ```
    
    ### Comments
    
    Minimal comments. Prefer self-documenting code. Comment "why", not "what":
    
    ```python
    # Good: explains rationale
    # Use pre-padding so recent transactions are at the end for LSTM
    X_train_seq = pad_sequences(train_sequences, padding='pre')
    
    # Bad: states the obvious
    # Loop through users
    for user_id in user_ids:
        ...
    ```
    
    ## Architecture
    
    ### Data Flow
    
    ```
    data/user_transactions/USER_XXXXXX.csv   ← per-user transaction CSVs
              ↓  TemporalTransactionFeatureEngineer.extract_all_features()
    data/user_features.csv                    ← user-level aggregate features
    data/user_labels.csv                      ← credit risk labels + loan metadata
              ↓  CreditRiskDataLoader
         train/test splits
              ↓
      LogisticRegressionModel / XGBoostModel / RandomForestModel / LightGBMModel
      LSTMModel / HybridLSTMModel
    ```
    
    ### Key Classes
    
    - **`TemporalTransactionFeatureEngineer`** — Extracts 8 feature categories from transactions
    - **`CalibratedMoMoDataGenerator`** — Generates synthetic mobile money data with loan behavior
    - **`CreditRiskDataLoader`** — Handles data loading, merging, splitting, validation, and loan feature engineering
    - **`LogisticRegressionModel`**, **`XGBoostModel`**, **`RandomForestModel`**, **`LightGBMModel`**, **`LSTMModel`**, **`HybridLSTMModel`** — Shared interface: `fit()`, `predict()`, `predict_proba()`, `cross_validate()`, `save()`, `load()`
    - **`ModelEvaluator`** — Collects predictions, generates comparison tables/plots
    
    ### Credit Archetypes
    
    The `CalibratedMoMoDataGenerator` assigns users to behavioral archetypes:
    
    | Archetype | Weight | Behavior |
    |-----------|--------|----------|
    | `non_borrower` | 40% | Never takes loans |
    | `responsible_borrower` | 35% | Takes loans, always repays on time |
    | `occasional_borrower` | 15% | Infrequent loans, variable repayment |
    | `risky_borrower` | 8% | Takes loans near limit, sometimes late |
    | `defaulter` | 2% | Takes loans, fails to repay |
    
    ### Target Conventions
    
    - `credit_risk_label`: `-1` = no loans, `0` = good, `1` = late, `2` = default
    - Non-borrowers (`-1`) excluded from training
    - Binary target: default (`label==2`) = 1, non-default (0 or 1) = 0
    - Currency: Ghanaian Cedi (GHS)
    
    ### Transaction Types
    
    `TRANSFER`, `DEBIT`, `PAYMENT`, `PAYMENT_SEND`, `CASH_OUT`, `CASH_IN`, `ADJUSTMENT`, `CREDIT` (loan disbursement), `LOAN_REPAYMENT`
    
    ## Key Patterns
    
    ### Random Seed
    
    Always use `RANDOM_SEED = 42`. Call `set_random_seeds()` before training:
    
    ```python
    def set_random_seeds(seed=RANDOM_SEED):
        np.random.seed(seed)
        tf.random.set_seed(seed)
        random.seed(seed)
    ```
    
    ### Data Loader Pattern
    
    **Call `prepare_static_splits()` before `load_sequences()`** to ensure shared train/test user IDs:
    
    ```python
    loader = CreditRiskDataLoader()
    splits = loader.prepare_static_splits()  # Sets train/test user IDs
    seq_data = loader.load_sequences()       # Uses same split
    ```
    
    ### Loan Features
    
    The `CreditRiskDataLoader._engineer_loan_features()` method computes 9 loan-specific features from raw transaction CSVs:
    - `total_loan_volume`, `avg_loan_amount`, `max_loan_amount`
    - `loan_to_total_volume_ratio`, `pct_credit_transactions`
    - `loan_timing_in_sequence`
    - `avg_balance_at_loan`, `min_balance_at_loan`, `balance_to_loan_ratio_at_disbursement`
    
    These features are not in `user_features.csv` because they depend on CREDIT/LOAN_REPAYMENT transaction types.
    
    ### Caching
    
    LSTM sequences are cached to `data/lstm_sequences.npz` after first load. The file is not tracked in git — delete it to force regeneration.
    
    ### Model Persistence
    
    All 6 model classes support `save(path)` / `load(path)`. Static models use joblib; Keras models use Keras native format + a companion `.json` for hyperparameters. Use `MODELS_DIR` from `config.py` as the save destination.
    
    ## File Locations
    
    ```
    src/seqcredit/          ← Source package
    notebooks/                    ← Jupyter notebooks
      model.ipynb          ← Primary modeling notebook (all 6 models)
      analysis.ipynb       ← Research analysis (y_bad, SHAP, surrogate tree, calibration)
      data.ipynb           ← Descriptive statistics
    src/
      synthetic_params.json       ← Synthetic data params (preserved)
    data/
      user_transactions/          ← Per-user CSVs (gitignored, regenerable)
      user_features.csv           ← Aggregated features
      user_labels.csv             ← User summaries with labels
      cv_results_y_default.csv    ← 5-fold CV results (primary target)
      cv_results_y_bad.csv        ← 5-fold CV results (secondary target)
      ablation_features.csv       ← Feature group ablation results
      tuning_results.csv          ← Hyperparameter tuning results
    models/                       ← Persisted trained models (created by model.save())
    ```
    
    ## Documentation Maintenance
    
    **When `data/cv_results_y_default.csv` or `data/cv_results_y_bad.csv` change** (after rerunning CV benchmark):
    
    1. Update `docs/PROJECT.md` — "Current Results" tables
    2. Update `README.md` — Results table
    
    **When `data/ablation_features.csv` changes:**
    
    1. Update `docs/PROJECT.md` — add/update ablation results section
    
    **When `data/tuning_results.csv` changes:**
    
    1. Update `docs/PROJECT.md` — note tuned model scores
    # AGENTS.md
    
    Guidance for coding agents working in this repository.
    
    ## Branch Reality
    
    The current branch is `real-data`, but the repo still contains the full local synthetic benchmark pipeline. Document and edit against the current codebase, not against older synthetic-only docs or paper drafts.
    
    ## Setup
    
    ```bash
    python -m venv .venv
    .venv\Scripts\activate        # Windows
    # source .venv/bin/activate   # macOS/Linux
    
    pip install -r requirements.txt
    pip install -e .
    ```
    
    `pip install -e .` is required for `python -m seqcredit.*` commands and notebook imports.
    
    ## Main Workflows
    
    ### Synthetic benchmark workflow
    
    ```bash
    python -m seqcredit.synthesize
    python -m seqcredit.pipeline
    jupyter notebook notebooks/model.ipynb
    ```
    
    Optional synthetic evaluation scripts:
    
    ```bash
    python -m seqcredit.run_cv_benchmark
    python -m seqcredit.run_ablation_study
    python -m seqcredit.run_hyperparameter_tuning
    python -m seqcredit.run_full_benchmark
    ```
    
    ### Real-data workflow
    
    The Databricks-oriented pipeline lives in `src/seqcredit/real_data_pipeline.py`. Its public entrypoint is:
    
    ```python
    from seqcredit.real_data_pipeline import build_pipeline
    ```
    
    Use it from a Spark notebook, for example:
    
    ```python
    df = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM melodatabricks616.default.yara_dump_table")
    build_pipeline(df, output_dir=None, min_followup_days=60)
    ```
    
    Do not assume real-data experiments are reproducible locally from this repo alone.
    
    ## Core Modules
    
    - `config.py`
      Central path constants plus runtime override helpers for data, labels, and sequence cache files.
    - `synthesize.py`
      `CalibratedMoMoDataGenerator` for synthetic transaction generation.
    - `pipeline.py`
      `TemporalTransactionFeatureEngineer` plus the synthetic user-feature build path.
    - `credit_model.py`
      `CreditRiskDataLoader`, metric helpers, evaluator, and all model classes.
    - `real_data_pipeline.py`
      Spark feature/label pipeline for the Telecel workflow.
    
    ## Models In Code
    
    Exported package models:
    
    - `LogisticRegressionModel`
    - `XGBoostModel`
    - `RandomForestModel`
    - `LightGBMModel`
    - `LSTMModel`
    - `GRUModel`
    - `HybridLSTMModel`
    - `HybridGRUModel`
    
    Additional classes also exist in `credit_model.py`:
    
    - `TransformerModel`
    - `HybridTransformerModel`
    
    For current benchmark results and research direction, refer to `docs/research.md` instead of duplicating metrics in operational docs.
    
    ## Data Conventions
    
    - Synthetic raw transactions: `data/user_transactions/USER_XXXXXX.csv`
    - Synthetic labels: `data/user_labels.csv`
    - Synthetic user features: `data/user_features.csv`
    - Sequence cache: `data/lstm_sequences.npz`
    - Raw real-data sequence cache path: `RAW_SEQ_FILE` in `config.py`
    
    Target conventions:
    
    - `credit_risk_label = -1`: non-borrower
    - `credit_risk_label = 0`: good
    - `credit_risk_label = 1`: late / risky
    - `credit_risk_label = 2`: default
    
    Training conventions in the synthetic pipeline:
    
    - non-borrowers are excluded
    - `y_default`: `label == 2`
    - `y_bad`: `label in {1, 2}`
    
    ## Important Patterns
    
    ### Split order
    
    Call `prepare_static_splits()` before `load_sequences()` so static and sequential data share the same user split.
    
    ### Runtime path overrides
    
    `config.py` supports runtime overrides through:
    
    - `SEQCREDIT_DATA_DIR`
    - `SEQCREDIT_LSTM_CACHE_FILE`
    - `SEQCREDIT_RAW_SEQ_FILE`
    - `SEQCREDIT_USER_FEATURES_FILE`
    - `SEQCREDIT_USER_LABELS_FILE`
    - `SEQCREDIT_EPHEMERAL`
    
    These matter for Databricks and temporary benchmark runs.
    
    ### Cleanup
    
    Use the reset utility instead of manual ad hoc deletion:
    
    ```bash
    python -m seqcredit.reset
    python -m seqcredit.reset --data --models --yes
    python -m seqcredit.reset --data-full --yes
    ```
    
    ## Documentation Rules
    
    When updating docs:
    
    - keep hardcoded benchmark facts and research conclusions in `docs/research.md`
    - keep `README.md` and `docs/PROJECT.md` focused on setup, workflows, code surface, and data conventions
    - keep `README.md`, `docs/PROJECT.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `CLAUDE.md` aligned
    - do not duplicate metric tables across markdown files
    
    ## Documentation Sync Points
    
    When result artifacts or notebook result sources change, update `docs/research.md` first:
    
    - `data/cv_results_y_default.csv`
    - `data/cv_results_y_bad.csv`
    - `data/ablation_features.csv`
    - `data/tuning_results.csv`
    - `data/significance_tests.csv`
    - `data/cv_manifest.json`

## Assistant

The two model folders are separate Git clones on different branches, and both retain a synthetic workflow. The larger `seqcredit-model-real` clone also contains the dashboard, publication archive, and tests.

I found some concrete cleanup issues: a root launcher points to a missing `seqcredit-mvp` folder, Git still records a stale worktree, and temporary test artifacts were committed and now show as deleted. I’m checking folder sizes and backup contents before recommending what to keep or archive.

    # seqcredit Presentation MVP
    
    This isolated project creates a small, fully synthetic mobile-money transaction
    dataset whose **broad benchmark pattern** resembles the archived real-data
    study: order-aware features should modestly outperform aggregate features for
    strict-default discrimination. It does not reconstruct Telecel records, reproduce
    the real experiment, or produce probabilities suitable for lending decisions.
    
    ## Current milestone: synthetic calibration
    
    The calibration target is intentionally approximate:
    
    | Quantity | Archived real reference | Synthetic acceptance band |
    |---|---:|---:|
    | Strict-default prevalence | 4.13% | 3.5%-5.0% |
    | Strongest static AUC-ROC | 0.721 | 0.70-0.74 |
    | Order-aware AUC-ROC | 0.752 | 0.735-0.77 |
    | Order-aware gain | about 0.03 | 0.015-0.05 |
    
    The synthetic model is an order-aware sklearn surrogate, not a GRU or LSTM.
    The dashboard must display the archived benchmark and synthetic demonstration
    as separate evidence.
    
    ## Run
    
    From this directory:
    
    ```powershell
    python -m pip install -e .
    python -m seqcredit_mvp.calibrate
    python -m seqcredit_mvp.scoring data/sample_transactions.csv
    streamlit run src/seqcredit_mvp/streamlit_app.py
    python -m pytest
    ```
    
    After dependencies are installed, launch the **Streamlit dashboard** with:
    
    ```powershell
    .\run_streamlit.ps1
    ```
    
    From the repository root, the same dashboard can be launched with:
    
    ```powershell
    streamlit run streamlit_app.py
    ```
    
    For Streamlit Community Cloud, use `streamlit_app.py` as the main file path.
    
    The calibration command writes:
    
    - `artifacts/static_model.joblib`
    - `artifacts/sequence_model.joblib`
    - `artifacts/manifest.json`
    - `data/benchmark_results.csv`
    - `data/sample_transactions.csv`
    
    All generated identifiers and transactions are fabricated.
    
    ## Input CSV schema
    
    Each row is one fabricated transaction. The required columns are:
    
    | Column | Meaning |
    |---|---|
    # Research Direction
    
    This note is intentionally lightweight. Current benchmark numbers, ablation
    findings, and the active real-data research narrative live in `docs/research.md`.
    
    ## Direction
    
    The branch contains both a synthetic benchmark pipeline and a Databricks
    real-data pipeline. The current research direction is led by the real-data
    workflow.
    
    Near-term work should focus on:
    
    - keeping the real-data pipeline leakage-aware, with features before the index
      loan and labels after it
    - validating the recurrent-model direction across reruns and runtime variation
    - improving recurrent-model calibration
    - deciding whether real-data notebook outputs should become tracked artifacts
      with a manifest
    - fixing Notebook C into a clean single rerun notebook for the A+B workflow
    
    ## Documentation Rule
    
    Do not duplicate hardcoded benchmark tables or ablation numbers here. Link to
    `docs/research.md` for current research facts.

    FILE: README.md
    # SME Credit Insight
    
    **Transaction evidence for SME and micro-credit professionals.**
    
    Upload transaction records, inspect financial patterns and data limitations,
    and export an evidence brief with the professional's own notes. The financial
    expert makes the lending decision in their institution's workflow.
    
    This is a standalone project starter, with no dependency on the old seqcredit
    repositories, proprietary data, trained prediction models, or Databricks.
    The ZIP also preserves **both original source instances** under `reference/`:
    `seqcredit/` (synthetic) and `seqcredit-model-real/` (real-data branch,
    including its synthetic path and existing presentation-app source). Their
    source is retained for feature migration; the new application runs independently.
    The default demonstration contains 693 fabricated transactions across three
    fabricated businesses and 120 calendar days.
    
    ## Start here
    
    Use Python 3.11 or later. Python 3.13 was used for the release checks.
    From this directory on Windows:
    
    ```powershell
    python -m venv .venv
    .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
    python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
    python -m streamlit run streamlit_app.py
    ```
    
    On macOS/Linux, activate with `source .venv/bin/activate` instead. Open the
    localhost URL printed by Streamlit. The default configuration binds to
    `127.0.0.1`; it does not expose the prototype on the local network.
    After installation, `./run.ps1` is a Windows launch shortcut.
    
    No API keys or cloud accounts are needed. Package installation needs internet
    access; analysis itself runs locally without external service calls.
    
    ## What works now
    
    - CSV upload with strict validation; no silently dropped or imputed rows.
    - Multiple businesses and accounts, reviewed one business at a time.
    - Recorded external inflows, outflows, net flow and monthly breakdowns.
    - Two 30-day comparison windows with coverage and denominator checks.
    - Counterparty concentration with an explicit known-inflow denominator.
    - Transaction category breakdowns and account-level balance observations.
    - Evidence-linked observations and questions for the professional.
    - Session-only professional notes, kept separate from calculated evidence.
    - Printable standalone HTML report, JSON evidence bundle and monthly CSV.
    - File fingerprint and calculation version for traceability.
    
    There is no credit score, default prediction, approve/decline output, risk
    band, recommended loan amount, or automated claim about repayment capacity.
    The starter uses deterministic calculations rather than a trained model or
    generative AI. This makes the initial analytical contract easy to verify.
    
    ## Use your own file
    
    Choose **Upload transaction CSV** in the sidebar. Start from
    [`sample_data/upload_template.csv`](sample_data/upload_template.csv) and read
    [`docs/INPUT_SCHEMA.md`](docs/INPUT_SCHEMA.md). Raw provider statements need an
    explicit format adapter; PDF/OCR, column mapping and bank connectors are future
    work. The supplied format supports one currency per business and separate
    `in`/`out` direction with non-negative amounts.
    
    ## Offline command-line reports
    
    Install the project as a package to use the CLI:
    
    ```powershell
    python -m pip install -e .
    sme-insight sample_data/fabricated_transactions.csv --business DEMO_MARKET_SHOP --output reports
    ```
    
    This writes `reports/evidence.html` and `reports/evidence.json`. Reusing the same
    output directory replaces those two files. HTML can be printed to PDF from a
    browser. [`examples/`](examples/) contains a fabricated example report.
    
    ## Tests and sample regeneration
    
    ```powershell
    python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
    python scripts/generate_sample.py
    ```
    
    The calculation/report tests use Python's standard library. The dashboard
    checks additionally use Streamlit's AppTest and skip if Streamlit is absent.
    The tests verify exact cash flows, internal-transfer handling, window
    boundaries, business separation, missing data, zero denominators, export
    escaping, dashboard rendering and note isolation when switching businesses.
    
    ## Project map
    
    ```text
    streamlit_app.py          Dashboard entry point
    src/sme_insight/
      analysis.py            Input validation, evidence metrics, observations
      dashboard.py           Upload, views, professional notes, downloads
      reporting.py           HTML / JSON / CSV exports
      cli.py                 Offline report command
    sample_data/             Fabricated demonstration and upload template
    examples/                Fabricated exported evidence report
    tests/                   Calculation, validation, export and UI checks
    scripts/                 Sample generation and release packaging
    docs/                    Scope, methods, handoff, submission and evaluation
    reference/               Both original source instances, tests and notebook code
    ```
    
    ## New repository and submission
    
    Unzip into a new folder, install and test, then initialize a fresh repository:
    
    ```powershell
    git init
    git add .
    git commit -m "Start transaction evidence workspace for SME credit review"
    ```
    
    No existing Git history is included. Read
    [`docs/PROJECT_BRIEF.md`](docs/PROJECT_BRIEF.md) for the agreed product scope,
    [`docs/SUBMISSION_BRIEF.md`](docs/SUBMISSION_BRIEF.md) for submission framing,
    and [`docs/HANDOFF.md`](docs/HANDOFF.md) for priorities and release details.
    For the behavioral features that differ between instances, start with
    [`docs/FEATURE_COMPARISON.md`](docs/FEATURE_COMPARISON.md) and the line-linked
    [`docs/FEATURE_INVENTORY.csv`](docs/FEATURE_INVENTORY.csv).
    
    ## Prototype boundary
    
    This is a local, runnable foundation. It has no authentication, persistent
    case store, source-statement verification, or institutional decision workflow.
    Uploaded data and notes are held in the running session; the app does not save
    them to disk. Downloads are deliberate local exports. This does not guarantee
    secure deletion from browser caches, OS memory or swap. See
    [`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) before adapting it for hosted use.
    
    New starter source is provided under the MIT license in `LICENSE`. Original
    reference sources retain their included notices; the starter's license does not
    replace those notices. Dependency licenses remain with their respective packages. Provenance and exclusions are
    documented in [`docs/PROVENANCE.md`](docs/PROVENANCE.md).
    
    FILE: docs/PROVENANCE.md
    # Provenance and exclusions
    
    This starter was created on 2026-10-19 from the user's requested change in
    direction after reviewing the local seqcredit project. The previous work
    informed the product problem and the need to separate evidence from decisions.
    
    The active application's source, tests, documentation, fabricated data generator
    and report templates are new implementations for this scope. At the user's
    explicit request, `reference/` also includes copies of both original source
    instances, supporting metadata and tests. The existing real-data presentation
    app source is included as well. No old dependency environment is bundled.
    
    `reference/SNAPSHOT_MANIFEST.json` records origin, SHA-256 and transformation
    for each archived file. Python modules and supporting files are byte-identical
    copies. Notebook snapshots preserve code cells while removing output payloads,
    execution counts, metadata, attachments and non-code cells. They are stored in
    `notebook_source/` to distinguish them from executed research evidence.
    
    ## Deliberately excluded
    
    - Real financial data, including the small Telecel sample and hashed IDs.
    - Trained models, pickle/joblib artifacts, neural-network weights and caches.
    - Executed notebook output payloads, raw transaction CSVs, saved benchmark CSVs
      and model artifacts. Archived source/docs may contain historical metrics and
      assertions; they remain reference material, not claims about the new app.
    - Old papers, reviewer PDFs, publication backups and third-party templates.
    - Git history, remote configuration, credentials, local secrets and environments.
    
    The fabricated data uses deterministic seed 42. Its identifiers begin with
    `DEMO_`; its records were generated without reading or fitting any real source
    data. It is not calibrated to reproduce the old project's predictive metrics.
    The generated example reports use only these fabricated transactions.
    
    The root MIT license applies to newly created starter files, not as a replacement
    for the original reference files' notices. Original LICENSE/notice files are
    preserved alongside the reference sources. Streamlit, pandas and
    their transitive dependencies retain their own licenses; package installation
    does not transfer those licenses to the project owner. Add final organization
    and author attribution when preparing the new repository for distribution.
    
    FILE: docs/HANDOFF.md
    # New project handoff
    
    ## Scope carried forward
    
    Users supply transactions. The application produces descriptive financial
    evidence. A professional reviews that evidence, obtains context and makes the
    lending decision in the institution's workflow. The existing prediction
    research is background, not a validation claim for the new application.
    
    ## Included in the archive
    
    Runnable Streamlit application; standalone analytical engine and CLI; upload
    contract; fabricated data and generator; example HTML/JSON reports; calculation
    and UI tests; local configuration; packaging utility; MIT license; architecture,
    methods, product brief, evaluation plan and draft submission framing.
    Both original instances are preserved under `reference/`, including their
    Python source, synthetic parameters, tests, dependency metadata, supporting
    docs and code-only notebook snapshots. The real-data instance also includes
    the existing presentation-app source, tests and configuration. Feature
    differences and definition mismatches are mapped in `docs/FEATURE_COMPARISON.md`
    and `docs/FEATURE_INVENTORY.csv`.
    
    The top-level `MANIFEST.sha256` lists checksums for all packaged project files
    except itself. The ZIP has a sibling `.sha256` checksum file. Neither file is
    a digital signature or source authentication.
    
    ## Suggested next work
    
    1. Run the app and inspect the fabricated demonstration with a financial
       professional. Confirm the evidence they need and language they understand.
    2. Confirm the intended submission's requirements and whether an analytics
       prototype fits the chosen track.
    3. Agree a real transaction export format and build one tested adapter. Keep
       direction, reversals, timezones and categories explicit.
    4. Add fabricated challenge cases and independent reference calculations.
    5. Conduct the proposed professional evaluation and report only observed results.
    6. Specify applicant/staff roles, storage, retention and sign-off if moving
       from this local starter to a hosted service.
    
    ## Environment and packaging
    
    `requirements.txt` and `pyproject.toml` declare compatible dependency ranges.
    `requirements-tested.txt` records exact direct dependency versions used during
    release verification; it is not a complete transitive lockfile. For a shared
    deployment, resolve and commit a complete environment lock after selecting the
    target Python version and host.
    
    To regenerate the fabricated examples, install the package and run:
    
    ```powershell
    python scripts/generate_sample.py
    python -m sme_insight.cli sample_data/fabricated_transactions.csv --business DEMO_MARKET_SHOP --output examples
    ```
    
    To rebuild the release after changes:
    
    ```powershell
    python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
    python scripts/package_release.py
    ```
    
    The packager includes only an explicit project-file allowlist and rejects
    symlinks. It excludes virtual environments, caches, uploads, working reports,
    Git metadata and arbitrary unlisted files. `examples/` is for the supplied
    fabricated output only. Never replace its fixtures with real customer data.
    Reference entries are checked against their snapshot hashes when packaging.
    
    No remote repository has been created or published. No existing source project
    was modified as part of producing this starter.

    ## Running Code

    ```bash
    jupyter notebook notebooks/model.ipynb
    ```
    
    **Full pipeline (generates transactions, labels, and features):**
    ```bash
    # Step 1: Generate synthetic transaction data + labels
    python -m seqcredit.synthesize
    
    # Step 2: Build user-level features from transactions
    python -m seqcredit.pipeline
    
    # Step 3: Run the modeling notebook
    jupyter notebook notebooks/model.ipynb
    ```
    
    **Incremental updates:**
    - Rebuild only features: `python -m seqcredit.pipeline`
    - Rebuild only transactions (regenerates both transactions and labels): `python -m seqcredit.synthesize`
    
    ## Lint & Typecheck
    
    ```bash
    # Linting and formatting
    ruff check src/
    ruff format src/
    
    # Type checking
    mypy src/ --ignore-missing-imports
    ```
    
    ## Tests
    
    No test suite exists.
    
    ## Code Style
    
    ### Imports
    
    Organize imports: stdlib → third-party → local. Use try/except for local imports:
    
    ```python
    from pathlib import Path
    from typing import Tuple, Dict, List, Optional
    
    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd
    
    try:
        from seqcredit.config import USER_FEATURES_FILE
    except ModuleNotFoundError:
        from config import USER_FEATURES_FILE
    ```
    
    ### Type Hints
    
    Required for public functions. Use standard library types and numpy/pandas:
    
    ```python
    def load_static_data(self) -> Tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.Series]:
        ...
    
    def predict_proba(self, X) -> np.ndarray:
        ...
    
    def _compute_class_weights(y: np.ndarray) -> Dict[int, float]:
        ...
    ```
    
    ### Docstrings
    
    Use triple-quoted Google-style docstrings:
    
    ```python
    def extract_all_features(self, df, windows=[3, 7, 14, 30]):
        """
        Extract complete feature set from transaction sequence.
    
        Args:
            df: DataFrame with columns [TRANSACTION DATE, AMOUNT, TRANS. TYPE,
                BAL BEFORE, BAL AFTER, etc.]
            windows: List of rolling window sizes (in days)
    
        Returns:
            DataFrame with engineered features
        """
        ...
    ```
    
    ### Naming Conventions
    
    - **Functions/variables**: `snake_case` (e.g., `load_static_data`, `train_indices`)
    - **Classes**: `PascalCase` (e.g., `CreditRiskDataLoader`, `LSTMModel`)
    - **Constants**: `UPPER_CASE` (e.g., `RANDOM_SEED`, `LSTM_FEATURE_COLUMNS`)
    - **Private methods**: Prefix with underscore (e.g., `_engineer_loan_features`)
    
    ### Module Structure
    
    Define constants at top, then classes, then standalone functions:
    
    ```python
    RANDOM_SEED = 42
    LSTM_FEATURE_COLUMNS = [...]
    
    class MyClass:
        ...
    
    def standalone_function():
        ...
    
    if __name__ == "__main__":
        main()
    ```
    
    ### Error Handling
    
    Use try/except with specific exceptions. Print warnings for recoverable errors:
    
    ```python
    try:
        df_user = pd.read_csv(filepath)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  [SKIP] {user_id}: could not read file ({e})")
        continue
    ```
    
    ### Logging
    
    Currently uses `print()` for output. Continue that pattern for progress messages:
    
    ```python
    print(f"Processed {i+1}/{total} users...")
    ```
    
    ### Comments
    
    Minimal comments. Prefer self-documenting code. Comment "why", not "what":
    
    ```python
    # Good: explains rationale
    # Use pre-padding so recent transactions are at the end for LSTM
    X_train_seq = pad_sequences(train_sequences, padding='pre')
    
    # Bad: states the obvious
    # Loop through users
    for user_id in user_ids:
        ...
    ```
    
    ## Architecture
    
    ### Data Flow
    
    ```
    data/user_transactions/USER_XXXXXX.csv   ← per-user transaction CSVs
              ↓  TemporalTransactionFeatureEngineer.extract_all_features()
    data/user_features.csv                    ← user-level aggregate features
    data/user_labels.csv                      ← credit risk labels + loan metadata
              ↓  CreditRiskDataLoader
         train/test splits
              ↓
      LogisticRegressionModel / XGBoostModel / RandomForestModel / LightGBMModel
      LSTMModel / HybridLSTMModel
    ```
    
    ### Key Classes
    
    - **`TemporalTransactionFeatureEngineer`** — Extracts 8 feature categories from transactions
    - **`CalibratedMoMoDataGenerator`** — Generates synthetic mobile money data with loan behavior
    - **`CreditRiskDataLoader`** — Handles data loading, merging, splitting, validation, and loan feature engineering
    - **`LogisticRegressionModel`**, **`XGBoostModel`**, **`RandomForestModel`**, **`LightGBMModel`**, **`LSTMModel`**, **`HybridLSTMModel`** — Shared interface: `fit()`, `predict()`, `predict_proba()`, `cross_validate()`, `save()`, `load()`
    - **`ModelEvaluator`** — Collects predictions, generates comparison tables/plots
    
    ### Credit Archetypes
    
    The `CalibratedMoMoDataGenerator` assigns users to behavioral archetypes:
    
    | Archetype | Weight | Behavior |
    |-----------|--------|----------|
    | `non_borrower` | 40% | Never takes loans |
    | `responsible_borrower` | 35% | Takes loans, always repays on time |
    | `occasional_borrower` | 15% | Infrequent loans, variable repayment |
    | `risky_borrower` | 8% | Takes loans near limit, sometimes late |
    | `defaulter` | 2% | Takes loans, fails to repay |
    
    ### Target Conventions
    
    - `credit_risk_label`: `-1` = no loans, `0` = good, `1` = late, `2` = default
    - Non-borrowers (`-1`) excluded from training
    - Binary target: default (`label==2`) = 1, non-default (0 or 1) = 0
    - Currency: Ghanaian Cedi (GHS)
    
    ### Transaction Types
    
    `TRANSFER`, `DEBIT`, `PAYMENT`, `PAYMENT_SEND`, `CASH_OUT`, `CASH_IN`, `ADJUSTMENT`, `CREDIT` (loan disbursement), `LOAN_REPAYMENT`
    
    ## Key Patterns
    
    ### Random Seed
    
    Always use `RANDOM_SEED = 42`. Call `set_random_seeds()` before training:
    
    ```python
    def set_random_seeds(seed=RANDOM_SEED):
        np.random.seed(seed)
        tf.random.set_seed(seed)
        random.seed(seed)
    ```
    
    ### Data Loader Pattern
    
    **Call `prepare_static_splits()` before `load_sequences()`** to ensure shared train/test user IDs:
    
    ```python
    loader = CreditRiskDataLoader()
    splits = loader.prepare_static_splits()  # Sets train/test user IDs
    seq_data = loader.load_sequences()       # Uses same split
    ```
    
    ### Loan Features
    
    The `CreditRiskDataLoader._engineer_loan_features()` method computes 9 loan-specific features from raw transaction CSVs:
    - `total_loan_volume`, `avg_loan_amount`, `max_loan_amount`
    - `loan_to_total_volume_ratio`, `pct_credit_transactions`
    - `loan_timing_in_sequence`
    - `avg_balance_at_loan`, `min_balance_at_loan`, `balance_to_loan_ratio_at_disbursement`
    
    These features are not in `user_features.csv` because they depend on CREDIT/LOAN_REPAYMENT transaction types.
    
    ### Caching
    
    LSTM sequences are cached to `data/lstm_sequences.npz` after first load. The file is not tracked in git — delete it to force regeneration.
    
    ### Model Persistence
    
    All 6 model classes support `save(path)` / `load(path)`. Static models use joblib; Keras models use Keras native format + a companion `.json` for hyperparameters. Use `MODELS_DIR` from `config.py` as the save destination.
    
    ## File Locations
    
    ```
    src/seqcredit/          ← Source package
    notebooks/                    ← Jupyter notebooks
      model.ipynb          ← Primary modeling notebook (all 6 models)
      analysis.ipynb       ← Research analysis (y_bad, SHAP, surrogate tree, calibration)
      data.ipynb           ← Descriptive statistics
    src/
      synthetic_params.json       ← Synthetic data params (preserved)
    data/
      user_transactions/          ← Per-user CSVs (gitignored, regenerable)
      user_features.csv           ← Aggregated features
      user_labels.csv             ← User summaries with labels
      cv_results_y_default.csv    ← 5-fold CV results (primary target)
      cv_results_y_bad.csv        ← 5-fold CV results (secondary target)
      ablation_features.csv       ← Feature group ablation results
      tuning_results.csv          ← Hyperparameter tuning results
    models/                       ← Persisted trained models (created by model.save())
    ```
    
    ## Documentation Maintenance
    
    **When `data/cv_results_y_default.csv` or `data/cv_results_y_bad.csv` change** (after rerunning CV benchmark):
    
    1. Update `docs/PROJECT.md` — "Current Results" tables
    2. Update `README.md` — Results table
